paper_title: Irrigation in India: Status and challenges

paper_identity.paper_title: Irrigation in India: Status and challenges

paper_summary: This viewpoint article reviews irrigation development in India, emphasizing the shift from canal toward tubewell-based irrigation, gaps between irrigation potential created and utilized, and environmental externalities including groundwater decline, salinization, waterlogging, erosion, sediment and chemical pollution, and nitrate contamination. It synthesizes secondary evidence on irrigation access heterogeneity across states and links irrigation to livelihood outcomes while arguing that technical and institutional measures remain insufficient relative to rising water stress.
study_region: India (national and multi-state statistics; secondary survey evidence cited for farm-plot irrigation status)
study_period: Long-run irrigation source mix (1951 versus 2012-13 cited); farm-plot irrigation status table from Songqing et al. (2012); policy and budget references through 2017-18
methodology: Viewpoint / narrative case-study synthesis with literature citations, secondary tabulated survey statistics (state-wise plot irrigation status), and qualitative environmental-impact review (no district/block-scale primary modeling in this paper).
paper_type_rationale: The manuscript is explicitly framed as a status-and-challenges viewpoint that synthesizes prior studies, national programme descriptions, and secondary statistics rather than presenting new identified causal estimates at fine spatial resolution.

key_relationships: Canal share of irrigation fell from 40% (1951) to 24% (2012-13) while well/tubewell share rose from 29% to 62% of total irrigated area (Fig. 1; Jeyaseelan 2014 as cited).

Ultimate irrigation potential revised upward: 113 million ha (1960s assessment) versus present status ~139 million ha, largely from minor groundwater and minor surface-water scheme reassessments (Manivanan 2006 as cited).
State heterogeneity in plot irrigation status (Table 1): Tamil Nadu high irrigation access versus Karnataka/Bihar/Jharkhand majority rainfed shares.
Irrigation-induced salinity drivers listed include poor on-farm WUE, canal seepage, and inadequate drainage (author synthesis).
Cited global statistic: ~10% irrigated land waterlogged with ~20% productivity decline in affected cropland (Mishra 2008 as cited).

alias_resolution_rules.notes: Mapped to groundwater level / depth trend per extraction prompt mandatory mappings.
Set medium=soil vs groundwater based on whether the paper refers to soil salt burden or irrigation-water/groundwater quality.
Taxonomy expansion includes explicit waterlogged-area construct.

mapping_notes: The paper is primarily a narrative review; several numeric claims are cited secondary/global statistics rather than new district/block estimates. Irrigation source-mix shares (canal vs tubewell) are interpretive context for dependence on groundwater irrigation but are not identical to irrigated_area_fraction (cropped-area irrigated share). Verification: mechanism_blocks stressor_scope updated where edges cross cluster_family; cluster_families_covered lists only families present on variables/edges (rainfed risk is discussed textually via irrigated vs rainfed shares but uses mixed cluster on irrigated_area_fraction). Edge e3 (salinity_level -> salinity_level) links groundwater-quality salinity forcing to soil salinity outcome; medium_scope=soil marks the soil-salinity endpoint.
limitations: No primary causal identification, limited quantification for India at block/district scale, and heavy reliance on cited syntheses and non-Indian farm studies for some productivity and reliability claims.

important_variables.significance: Central headline indicator (1-2 m/year) framing groundwater stress as a national consequence of irrigation-intensive development pathways.
Table 1 state-level plot irrigation status quantifies heterogeneity between irrigation access and rainfed dominance—critical context for water-scarcity exposure and policy targeting.
Soil and water-quality salinity are treated as core irrigation externalities with direct yield pathways via cited experimental work.
Groundwater nitrate survey ranges are used to connect irrigated intensification and N management to drinking-water quality risks.
Explicitly listed as a salinity driver, aligning irrigation management quality with salt accumulation mechanisms.

important_variables_narrative: The paper’s most decision-relevant quantities for scarcity mechanism discovery are the national groundwater decline headline (supporting groundwater_stress linkages to irrigation intensity), the Songqing et al. irrigation-access table (structuring rainfed versus irrigated exposure across states), and the salinity–yield and waterlogging–productivity narratives that connect irrigation infrastructure and management to agronomic outcomes. Nitrate-leaching discussion adds a groundwater-quality outcome chain under intensive irrigated nutrient management, though many numbers are cited rather than newly estimated within this article.
